title: Tiny Savoy Doing He Man's Job In Giving Men For Uncle Sam
text:
Tiny Savoy Doing He Man's Job In Giving Men For Uncle Sam

BY JOHN CLIFT
(Herald State Editor)

SAVOY— One of the smallest towns in North Texas is supplying one of the largest amounts of manpower for the armed forces in the nation. On a percentage basis, that is.

The latest head count in Savoy listed the population at 312. As of next week when Lewis Beckham reports to the air force at Lackland in San Antonio, some 33 Savoy residents will be currently in service.

"Somebody ought to give us an 'E' for excellence in supplying men for the armed forces," said Postmaster Claud Strickland, who, as postmaster, keeps probably as close a watch as anyone on men's immediate families.

Of Savoy men in service, two have been killed, both in the early days in service in Africa. They were Peter Farr, Pan Seals, and Wirt Terry.

However, another died overseas in World War I. He was Isaac Le Large, who succumbed to pneumonia.

SON-IN-LAWS, TOO

Several families have two or more sons in service and two families with one have additional male members 1-A.

Mrs. Fae Miller has two sons and a son-in-law in uniform. Sgt. Bill is in the air force at Laredo and Capt. Sam is now on his third overseas hitch, this time in Japan. The son-in-law is Joe Bailey Springfield, who also is in Japan.

The two Hensley boys, Eugene, who is in Germany and Henry, now stationed at Camp Dafter[?], are also in service. They are sons of Mr. and Mrs. Lester Hensley.

A son-in-law, Maj. Foy L. Shoemate, is serving in Japan.

Another brother combine is Harry and Jimmy Arterbery, both serving in Japan. They are the sons of Bob Elk.

One of the questions asked most frequently in Savoy is "when is the Korean war going to end?" It is asked not only by parents, but by everyone. When you take 33 servicemen out of a town of 312, you know that most families in the town are directly affected.

The Savoy boys have seen the world. Postmaster Strickland handles letters from all over the globe. "They've been in Greenland and Alaska," he said. "They have sent silk from China, cameos from Italy, and perfume from France, India, Germany, England, any place that America has sent troops a Savoy boy has been there," Strickland added.

Airman Max E. Arterbery's last letter to his parents, Mr. and Mrs. Max Arterbey, came from Matador Island in the Pacific. Earl Blakey, son of Earl Blakey. Is in the air force and is making some of the training flight over Korea.

Bascom Blount, son of Mr. and Mrs. Willie Blount, isn't far from home at Caswell AFB, N. C. Often, however, he frequently hops "almost around the world" as a B-36 crewman.

Naturally, a lot of the Savoy men are still getting stateside duty
